title: EIP-8198: Quick Slots
description: Introduce variable slot timing infrastructure and reduce slot duration.
author: Carl Beekhuizen (@carlbeek), Barnabé Monnot (@barnabemonnot), Barnabas Busa (@barnabasbusa)
bodyPreview: ## Abstract This EIP makes the slot duration a scheduled consensus-layer configuration — a `SLOT_DURATION_SCHEDULE` whose entries each activate a slot duration at an upgrade epoch — rather than a compile-time constant, then uses that infrastructure to reduce slot duration from twelve to ten seconds. Duration-dependent consensus quantities are rescaled by the exact slot-duration ratio, applied inline in each formula, so that issuance, penalties, and churn are unchanged per unit of wall-clock time, and the data column sidecar retention window is redefined in milliseconds so that it too is unchanged in wall-clock time. The execution layer is deliberately decoupled: it never consumes the slot duration, and gas and blob throughput per unit time are maintained through coordinated parameter updates around the transition. ## Motivation Slot time is the heartbeat of Ethereum's user experience. Every second shaved off means faster transaction landings, faster exchange deposits, and faster real-world payments. But the benefits extend well beyond UX. ### User experience Twelve seconds is slow. It is perceptible in payments, exchange deposits, and every on-chain interaction. Reducing slot time brings Ethereum closer to the responsiveness users already expect from modern financial infrastructure as well as other chains including L2s. ### DEX pricing and MEV Arbitrage losses of AMM liquidity providers scale roughly with the square root of the inter-block time. Going from twelve to ten seconds cuts them by about 9%, tightening on-chain pricing and reducing value extracted from users. MEV extraction is also non-linear in slot time: shorter slots compress the surplus available per block. ### Fast finality and fast confirmation rule Faster slots pull forward time-to-finality and time-to-fast-confirmation. As further improvements roll out on these metrics, faster slots compound the decreases. ### Censorship-resistance More block proposers per unit of time increases censorship resistance, giving more opportunities for transactions to be included in the chain. In particular, economic censorship resistance increases too, i.e., the cost of bribing sequential block proposers to "turn off" access of a transaction or all transactions to the chain. ### Preconfirmation complexity Preconfirmation protocols exist to paper over twelve-second latency. Reducing slot time attacks the root cause, decreasing the need for additional trust assumptions and protocol complexity layered on top. ### Rollups and interoperability L2s inherit the L1's slot duration for some of their interoperability. For instance, some L2s wait a certain number of blocks before processing user deposits, so L1 to L2 deposits and messages become faster in wall-clock time. Intent-based bridges also frequently wait for inclusion on L1 to fill a user order on a separate domain. Based rollups inherit L1 block time as their sequencing interval. Faster L1 slots mean faster based rollups, with zero changes required on the rollup side. ## Specification The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119) and [RFC 8174](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8174). All arithmetic in this specification uses integer division (truncating toward zero) unless otherwise noted. ### Parameters | Name | Kind | Value | | ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | | `HEZE_FORK_EPOCH` | Fork epoch | TBD | | `SLOT_DURATION_SCHEDULE` | New consensus-layer configuration | See [Slot duration schedule](#slot-duration-schedule) | | `MIN_BLOB_DATA_RETENTION_MS` | New networking configuration | `1572864000` (~18.2 days) | | `SLOT_DURATION_MS` | Deprecated configuration | Replaced by `SLOT_DURATION_SCHEDULE` | | `MIN_EPOCHS_FOR_DATA_COLUMN_SIDECARS_REQUESTS` | Deprecated configuration | Replaced by `MIN_BLOB_DATA_RETENTION_MS` | The *slot-duration ratio* at an epoch is the rational number `r = get_slot_duration_ms(epoch) / get_slot_duration_ms(GENESIS_EPOCH)`, `5/6` for the ten-second era. It is never evaluated on its own: a formula applying `r` or `r²` multiplies by the numerator and divides by the denominator last. ### Slot duration schedule `SLOT_DURATION_SCHEDULE` is a list of records, each holding only an activation epoch and a slot duration in milliseconds. It replaces the standalone `SLOT_DURATION_MS`; the helper `get_slot_duration_ms(epoch)` returns the duration in effect at `epoch`. The schedule MUST satisfy the following: - It MUST begin with an entry at `GENESIS_EPOCH` carrying the historical slot duration (12,000 ms). This entry is the baseline of the slot-duration ratio. - Entries MUST be sorted by epoch in strictly ascending order. - Every subsequent entry MUST activate at the epoch of a network upgrade, `HEZE_FORK_EPOCH` or later. Slot duration changes between upgrades are not supported; the upgrade's fork version separates the networking domains. - The slot duration in each entry MUST be a positive multiple of 1,000 ms, so that every slot boundary has an exact integer-second timestamp. On mainnet, this EIP adds an entry at `HEZE_FORK_EPOCH` with a slot duration of 10,000 ms. ### Intra-slot deadlines Intra-slot deadlines keep their existing configuration as basis points of the slot duration: the attestation, aggregate, sync message, and contribution deadlines and the proposer reorg cutoff (`ATTESTATION_DUE_BPS`, `PROPOSER_REORG_CUTOFF_BPS`, and so on), and any further deadlines defined by the forks active at `HEZE_FORK_EPOCH`, such as payload or inclusion list deadlines.
